# Kontext: EHL Finale (TUM.ai EHL Munich 2026, 10.–11.10.) – BMW Challenge

## Projekt
- Lokaler Ordner: ~/Documents/00_Events/EHL Finale
- Team-Repo: github.com/eklavyagoyal/ehl-finale-munich-submission (privat, Branch main, Teamkollegen pushen auch, vor Push immer fetchen/rebasen)
- Challenge: KI-App, die aus Kundenfeedback, BMW-Daten und Webrecherche Kundenanforderungen für das Nachfolgemodell (1er/5er/7er; EU/CN/US) ableitet, priorisiert und den Produktmanager entscheiden lässt (freigeben/ablehnen/bearbeiten). Ein Audit Trail protokolliert alles.
- Alle Infos zur Challenge stehen in docs/challenge/brief.md (Mission, Scope, Deliverables, 8 Pflichtfelder pro Requirement, BMW-Prozess mit Aufteilung KI vs. Mensch)

## Repo-Struktur (main)
- docs/README.md: Inhaltsverzeichnis
- docs/challenge/brief.md und sources/ (Briefing-PDF, 3 Slides)
- docs/datasets/: README (Übersicht, Abdeckung, Auffälligkeiten), customer-feedback.md, customer-studies.md, sales-volumes.md, option-lists/{F70-1-series,G60-5-series,G70-7-series}.md
- docs/bmw-pm-interview/: Notizen aus dem Gespräch mit dem BMW-Produktmanager (von Eklavya)
- data/: BMW-Rohdaten (8 Dateien aus Google Drive), per .gitignore NICHT im Repo
- .claude/settings.json und .entire/: lokal, gitignored (jeder richtet Entire selbst ein)

## Wichtige Erkenntnisse aus den Daten
- Feedback-Dateien: 1 Zeile pro Klassifizierung, nicht pro Feedback, also nach ID deduplizieren
- Kein Kundenfeedback für China und Deutschland; 5er/7er-Feedback kommt zu ~90 % aus den USA; Quellen B/C/D nur USA
- 1er (F70): nur Verkäufe in EU und Rest der Welt (keine in CN/US), nur Verbrenner
- G68 (5er Langversion, China) nur in der Kundenstudie und den Sales-Zahlen
- Kundenstudie: CN/EU = Mittelwerte (vermutlich Skala 1–10), USA = Verteilung auf 7-Punkte-Skala, nicht direkt vergleichbar, keine Stichprobengrößen
- Sales-Zahlen ohne Aufteilung nach Antrieb; 5er G60+G68 zusammengefasst
- OptionLists = deutsche Preislisten (Juli 2026); 7er-Ausstattungsdaten nur für 4 von 7 Modellen

## Entire (hack.entire.io/ehl-munich-2026)
- CLI 0.11.4 per Homebrew installiert; in EHL Finale aktiviert (Agent claude-code, Telemetrie an)
- `entire doctor` ist OK, aber: noch nicht eingeloggt (`entire login` selbst ausführen), 0 Checkpoints bisher
- Sessions nur im Repo- oder Worktree-Ordner starten; beim Commit „Commit mit Session verknüpfen?“ mit yes beantworten
- entire.io: Eklavya muss die GitHub App installieren und das Repo importieren

## Nächster Schritt
- Worktree mit eigenem Branch für die Entwicklung anlegen
- Dort fehlen data/, .claude/ und .entire/: data/ hineinkopieren (kein Symlink, den deckt /data/ in der .gitignore nicht ab), im Worktree `entire enable --agent claude-code` ausführen
- Dann Demo-Scope festlegen (Fahrzeug und Markt) und die Architektur planen

# BMW Challenge — AI for Product Decision Making

Everything BMW gave us about the challenge, consolidated in one place (EHL Munich 2026 final, TUM.ai, 10–11 Oct 2026).

**Sources** (originals in [`sources/`](sources/)):

| # | Source | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| S1 | [`BMW_Hackathon_Briefing_Short.pdf`](sources/BMW_Hackathon_Briefing_Short.pdf) | Official 2-page briefing (BMW Group) |
| S2 | Detailed mission text (shared by BMW, pasted by the team) | Sections 1–5: mission, scope, "make it yours", deliverables |
| S3 | [`slide-data-and-sources.png`](sources/slide-data-and-sources.png) | Table "Data and sources — provided data (per vehicle)" |
| S4 | [`slide-billions-of-findings-to-one-vehicle.webp`](sources/slide-billions-of-findings-to-one-vehicle.webp) | Slide "From billions of findings to one BMW vehicle" |
| S5 | [`slide-the-process.webp`](sources/slide-the-process.webp) | Slide "The process" (BMW's requirements workflow) |

Where S1 and S2 differ in wording or emphasis, both are kept and marked.

---

## 1. The challenge in one paragraph

*What should the next generation of a BMW vehicle offer its customers?* Build an AI-powered application that helps product managers (PMs) **derive, justify and prioritize customer requirements for a successor vehicle**. Ground the proposals in customer feedback, BMW product and sales data, and relevant web research, while keeping **the PM firmly in control of every decision**. (S1)

## 2. Why this matters (S1)

- Defining a new vehicle generation means understanding what customers value today **and** anticipating what they will value when the successor reaches the market.
- PMs turn large volumes of customer feedback, market signals, competitor information and product data into well-founded product requirements.
- Today this work is largely **manual, time-consuming and hard to trace consistently**.
- AI could help PMs identify relevant insights, formulate requirements and justify prioritization decisions more efficiently, while keeping **evidence, assumptions and uncertainties transparent and under human control**.

## 3. Mission

### 3.1 Short version (S1)

Develop an application that helps PMs **define, explain and prioritize customer-facing requirements for the successor of an existing BMW vehicle line**.

- **Vehicles:** BMW 1 Series, 5 Series, 7 Series, or a combination.
- **Markets:** Europe, China, the United States, or any subset that best demonstrates the approach.
- **Time horizon:** think **3–5 years ahead**. Which customer needs and expectations should shape the next generation?
- Make clear **where conclusions rest on available evidence and where they rely on forward-looking assumptions**.
- For each vehicle BMW provides **customer feedback, equipment data, sales volumes and a customer study**. Teams may enrich these with external sources (competitor information, reviews, market or technology trends).
- BMW cares about **how the solution turns diverse information into actionable PM insights and makes its reasoning transparent**, not about a specific workflow or technical architecture.

### 3.2 Detailed version (S2, section 1 "Your mission")

Build an AI-powered application that ingests heterogeneous data, derives customer requirements for a vehicle, prioritizes them, and puts a PM in the loop at the decisions that matter. The app should be able to:

1. **Ingest** the provided data and enrich it with structured knowledge from the web.
2. **Extract signals** such as recurring complaints, unmet needs, competitor advantages and market trends, **each linked to its sources**.
3. **Derive requirements** from those findings: clear, actionable, customer-facing and realistic.
4. **Prioritize** them with a logic we define and can explain.
5. **Involve the PM** to approve, reject, edit or challenge requirements, along with the rationale and evidence behind them.
6. **Record everything in an audit trail**: a complete, chronological record of all actions, changes and access events within the system.

## 4. Scope (S2, section 2)

| In scope: customer requirements on the product | Out of scope |
| --- | --- |
| Features and equipment | Regulatory and homologation requirements (e.g. safety, emissions, type approval) |
| Comfort and space | Technical and engineering requirements (e.g. component specs, architecture, supplier topics) |
| Usability | Pricing, business case and cost calculation. **Cost or effort may be used as a rough prioritization factor.** |
| Infotainment and digital services | |
| Design and quality perception | |
| Driving experience | |
| Range and charging **as experienced by the customer** | |
| Variant and package offering, etc. | |

S1 says the same in short form: focus on **customer value** rather than engineering specifications, regulatory requirements or detailed business-case calculations.

## 5. Make it yours

- Demonstrate the application for **at least one derivative in one market**. Don't design it as a one-off: it should be **adaptable to other BMW vehicles and markets**. The remaining datasets and scenarios are available for optional testing. (S2)
- The challenge is broad on purpose. Focus where the team can contribute most, for example (S1 + S2):
  - going deep on **web research** and turning external information into usable evidence,
  - integrating and interpreting the **provided BMW data**,
  - uncovering customer insights, formulating compelling requirements, improving prioritization,
  - designing an effective **human-in-the-loop** experience.
- Not every capability needs the same maturity, but **show how the chosen focus connects to the full path from evidence to PM decision**. (S2)
- Consider how the concept scales across vehicle lines, markets and future product decisions. (S1)
- **What BMW values (S1):** trustworthy sources, transparent reasoning, thoughtful prioritization, and a clear understanding of **uncertainty and conflicting evidence**.

## 6. Deliverables

### 6.1 What to demonstrate (S1)

- **A concept and working prototype** showing how AI supports the identification, formulation and prioritization of customer-facing requirements, using the provided data and, where relevant, external sources.
- **A representative set of requirements supported by clear evidence and reasoning.** Show how customer feedback, product data, market signals or competitor insights translate into requirements, and explain the factors driving their prioritization.
- **A transparent decision-support experience** that lets PMs review, challenge, modify, approve or reject AI proposals, with evidence, assumptions, uncertainties and key decisions visible and traceable throughout.

### 6.2 Expected deliverables (S2, section 5)

> S2 jumps from section 3 to section 5; its section 4 is empty in the source.

1. **Concept and demonstrable prototype** of an AI-powered product-requirements application that processes heterogeneous inputs, derives product requirements, supports prioritization and integrates human review.
2. **Structured sample list of derived product requirements.** Every requirement needs all of these fields:
   - [ ] Unique identifier
   - [ ] Clear, actionable description
   - [ ] Linked findings and sources
   - [ ] Priority or score
   - [ ] Applied prioritization rationale
   - [ ] Evidence level
   - [ ] Key future-facing assumptions and uncertainties
   - [ ] Current decision status
3. **Clearly defined end-to-end workflow** showing how inputs become proposed and prioritized requirements, **which activities the AI performs autonomously, and where human review is mandatory**.
4. **Demonstrable audit trail** that makes each requirement traceable from its findings and sources through consolidation, scoring, prioritization and human decision-making. It must record changes to requirement **content, scores, priorities, evidence and status**, including **who or what** initiated each change, **when**, and the **documented rationale**.

> Teams choose their own technical approach, architecture, prioritization logic and UX. The deliverables describe capabilities and outcomes, not a prescribed design. They can be one integrated solution or a set of connected concepts, prototypes, models and visualizations. (S2)

## 7. Provided data (S3)

"Provided data (per vehicle)":

| Dataset | What it contains | What it is good for | Our file(s) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Customer verbatims** | Free-text customer feedback on the current vehicle | Pain points, unmet needs, what customers love and must not lose | `*_feedback_hackathon.xlsx` |
| **Equipment list** | Standard and optional equipment by trim and market | What the car offers today, gaps against competitors | `*_OptionList.PDF` |
| **Sales volumes** | Units by powertrain and region | Where the car sells, which powertrains matter, where it underperforms | `sales_volumes.xlsx` |
| **Customer study** | Customer ratings in various categories | How customers perceive, like/dislike and rate different components of a car | `F70_G60_G68_G70_customer_studies.xlsx` |

Schemas, value distributions and quirks of each file: [`../datasets/`](../datasets/README.md).

## 8. BMW's framing: from findings to one car (S4)

![From billions of findings to one BMW vehicle](sources/slide-billions-of-findings-to-one-vehicle.webp)

**1 billion findings › 1,000 requirements › one car.**

> **Customer requirement = customer-relevant attribute of a car.**

- **Example findings (raw customer voice):** "Charging takes too long." · "The NEW XPENG." · "Too many menus." · "Ugly kidney grille." · "I love the design." · "Too much plastic." · "More rear space, please." · "Uncomfortable seats." · "The app should just work." · "Very nice exterior colors." · "Tesla and GROK"
- **Example requirement themes (word cloud):** affordable, easy updates, data privacy, safety, joy of driving, flexible storage, everyday space, efficiency, connected, design, great sound, easy charging, reliable software, clear displays, easy entry, seat ventilation, home charging, art app, **intuitive UX**, iconic design, comfortable seats, smooth ride, fast charging, fast app response, sport wheels, real-world range, easy parking, heated seats, long battery life, personalized, carbon roof, simple maintenance, clear navigation, low running costs, dynamic, room for family, sustainable, easy child seat fit, electric, physical controls, **premium feel**, **range**
- Visual: "Future BMW sedan" (AI concept visual).

Takeaway: the job is **condensing many noisy, overlapping findings into a manageable set of customer-relevant attributes**. The findings mix complaints, praise, competitor mentions (XPENG, Tesla, Grok) and trends.

## 9. BMW's requirements process (S5)

![The process](sources/slide-the-process.webp)

Five stages, left to right. The slide marks each box with a **robot icon (AI)** and/or a **person icon (human)**:

| Stage | Box | Content on the slide | AI | Human |
| --- | --- | --- | :---: | :---: |
| **1. Situation analysis** | Baseline | Previous BMW model · BMW portfolio · Sales volume | ✓ | ✓ |
| | Competition | | ✓ | |
| | Customer / public feedback | | ✓ | |
| | Product and global trends | | ✓ | |
| **2. Structure & context** | Classify, cluster, contextualize | "AI standardizes findings, identifies duplicates, groups themes and connects insights" | ✓ | |
| | All potential requirements (0/1) | e.g. BEV powertrain, cooler, seat ventilation, … → **"Implement requirement?"** (binary yes/no) | | |
| **3. Requirements definition** | Specification and quantification | "Define measurable targets and acceptance criteria" | ✓ | ✓ |
| | Metric specification | e.g. *Range: 600 or 700 mi?* · *Cooler: for how many bottles?* · *Seat ventilation: fast enough?* | | |
| | (unlabeled column, likely domains) | Exterior · Interior · Powertrain · Driver assistance · … | | |
| **4. Prioritization** | | Customer · Business · … | ✓ | ✓ |
| **5. Documentation** | Requirements tracking | (cycle icon: continuous tracking) | ✓ | |

Reading of the slide (our interpretation):

- **AI-only (autonomous) steps:** gathering competition, feedback and trends; classifying, clustering and de-duplicating findings; documentation and requirements tracking.
- **AI + human (review mandatory) steps:** setting the baseline, specifying and quantifying requirements, prioritization. These map directly onto deliverable 6.2 #3 ("where human review is mandatory").
- Requirements go through two levels: first a **binary decision** (implement: 0/1), then a **metric specification** (how much / how good).
- Prioritization weighs **customer** value against **business** factors.

## 10. Related inputs from BMW people

- Notes from the conversation with a BMW product manager: [`../bmw-pm-interview/`](../bmw-pm-interview/). It covers the signal channels, the prioritization questions BMW actually asks, the 1–2 year iteration loop, and how lines between vehicle classes are drawn.

## 11. Quick facts

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Vehicles (e-codes) | **F70** = 1 Series · **G60** = 5 Series sedan · **G68** = 5 Series long wheelbase (China; customer study only) · **G70** = 7 Series |
| Markets in focus | Europe, China, USA (any subset) |
| Horizon | Successor vehicle, 3–5 years ahead |
| Minimum demo | ≥ 1 derivative in ≥ 1 market, built to generalize |
| Hard constraints | Customer-facing requirements only; no regulatory, engineering or pricing work |
| Must-haves | Requirement list (8 fields), E2E workflow with AI-vs-human split, audit trail, PM-in-the-loop prototype |

Source: [Original conversation notes](conversation-with-bmw-prod-manager.md).

This document organizes the discussion into a foundation for our next steps. The source is a set of rough notes; examples and estimates below should be read in that context.

## Core idea

Product requirements develop through an ongoing process of gathering signals, understanding their relevance, checking feasibility, and refining a vehicle-specific draft. Decisions depend on the market, customer group, vehicle class, engineering possibilities, and business constraints.

The manager emphasized that this process keeps looping. The timeline mentioned was roughly **one to two years**, with repeated reviews and deeper investigation of internal feedback.

## Where the signals come from

The discussion identified several inputs:

- **Social media:** customer feedback and requests.
- **Agencies:** another channel for input; their specific role was not detailed.
- **Competitors:** comparisons of what other vehicles offer and how quickly competitors may catch up.
- **Market contacts:** people who understand local culture, customer habits, and everyday usability.
- **Internal feedback and usage data:** deeper feedback reviews, plus data supplied through the app and use of the car.

Before prioritizing a request, the manager pointed to the number of people behind it, its sources, source reliability, the relevant region, and the functionality involved. A verification loop was also mentioned, although its exact steps were not described.

## How the work progresses

The notes suggest the following flow, with repeated loops between stages:

1. **Collect signals** from the different channels.
2. **Assess relevance and priority**, including the market and any quality issues.
3. **Speak with engineering early** to establish rough feasibility: can the requirement actually be implemented?
4. **Align the inputs and constraints** into a first draft for the specific car.
5. **Revisit the draft**, investigate internal feedback more deeply, and update requirements as new information arrives.

The initial engineering conversation is an early feasibility check. The notes do not describe a formal approval process or fixed gates between these stages.

## What shapes a decision

| Area | Questions raised in the discussion |
| --- | --- |
| Evidence | How many people are asking? Which sources support the request, and how reliable are they? |
| Market fit | Which region is relevant? Does the requirement fit local culture and how people use the car? |
| Functionality and quality | What functionality is involved? What quality issues need attention? |
| Vehicle fit | Is the request reasonable for this class of car? Does it belong in a higher class? How do vehicle size and budget affect the decision? |
| Engineering and R&D | Can it be implemented? Is it feasible from an R&D perspective? |
| Cost and business case | Is it feasible cost-wise? What are the budget, volume, and margin considerations? |
| Reuse | Can the requirement or feature be used in other vehicles? |
| Timing and flexibility | How quickly could the requirement change? How does that fit the development timeline, and can the team stay flexible? |
| Competition | How does the vehicle compare with competitors? How quickly could they catch up? |

Finding the data needed to answer these questions was itself raised as a challenge.

## Differences between markets and vehicle lines

The manager described drawing boundaries between vehicle lines as tricky. No fixed rule was given; feasibility, vehicle size, budget, customer group, and competitor comparisons all influence the decision.

The notes include illustrative customer examples: younger people in relation to the **1 Series**, and entrepreneurs in relation to the **5 or 7 Series**. These are discussion examples, not a complete segmentation model.

The discussion also referred to **“product genesis”** and the contribution of people in each market who understand its culture and basic usability needs. Their input helps assess whether a requirement fits that market.

## Timeline and when the loop ends

When asked about the timeline and criteria for ending the loop, the answer remained somewhat unspecified. The discussion raised R&D feasibility, reuse across vehicles, budget, changing requirements, functionality, competition, region, volume, and margins as relevant considerations.

The notes do not establish a fixed number of iterations, a precise stopping rule, or a final decision owner.

## Internal data collection

When asked how data is collected internally, the manager referred to the **app** and **use of the car**, through which users supply data. The notes end before this process is explained further.

The specific data collected, how it is accessed, and how it feeds into prioritization remain unclear.

## Open questions for the next stage

- What does the verification loop check, and what evidence is sufficient to prioritize a request?
- How are conflicting signals from different sources and markets resolved?
- How are requests allocated between vehicle lines in practice?
- What determines when a draft is ready and the iteration loop can end? Who makes that decision?
- Which data is available for assessing demand, feasibility, cost, volume, and margins?
- How are app and vehicle-usage data connected to customer feedback and product decisions?

These are follow-up questions derived from gaps in the notes. They are not additional requirements stated by the manager.

---

## Ziel

Für jede sinnvolle Kombi aus Fahrzeug und Markt soll klar sein, gegen welche Fahrzeuge der Nachfolger antritt und was deren Kunden und die Fachpresse loben oder kritisieren. Die Ergebnisse sollen so strukturiert sein, dass wir sie später direkt mit dem BMW-Feedback vergleichen können. Im BMW-Prozess ist das der Schritt „Competition“, den die KI eigenständig erledigen soll.

## 1. Scope: 7 Kombis statt 9

Der 1er wird in China und den USA nicht verkauft, deshalb fallen diese beiden Kombis weg. Den 5er gibt es in China nur als Langversion G68. Er bekommt deshalb eigene Wettbewerber: Langversionen und chinesische E-Limousinen.

Die Wettbewerber in der Tabelle sind **Hypothesen**. Die Webrecherche soll sie bestätigen oder korrigieren.

| Kombi | Vermutete Wettbewerber |
| --- | --- |
| **F70 · EU** | Mercedes A-Klasse, Audi A3 Sportback, VW Golf (GTI/R vs. M135), Mini; elektrische Kompakte als Ausblick |
| **G60 · EU** | Mercedes E-Klasse / EQE, Audi A6 / A6 e-tron, Tesla |
| **G60 · US** | E-Class, A6, Genesis G80, Lexus ES, Tesla Model S/3, Cadillac CT5 |
| **G68 · CN** | E-Klasse L, Audi A6L, Xiaomi SU7, NIO ET7, Zeekr, Huawei-Marken (Luxeed), BYD Han |
| **G70 · EU** | S-Klasse / EQS, Audi A8, Porsche Panamera |
| **G70 · US** | S-Class / EQS, Lexus LS, Genesis G90, Lucid Air, Tesla Model S |
| **G70 · CN** | S-Klasse / Maybach, Audi A8L, Maextro S800, NIO ET9, Hongqi |

**Blick 3–5 Jahre voraus:** Der Nachfolger tritt gegen die *nächste* Generation der Wettbewerber an. Angekündigte Modelle nehmen wir deshalb mit auf und markieren sie als zukunftsbezogene Annahme. Das zahlt direkt auf das Pflichtfeld „Annahmen und Unsicherheiten“ ein.

## 2. Drei Evidenz-Ebenen pro Kombi

| Ebene | Inhalt | Quelle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **(a) Ausstattung** | Nur kundenrelevante Punkte aus dem Scope: Displays und Bedienung, Fahrassistenz, Reichweite und Laden aus Kundensicht, Platz im Fond, Sitzkomfort, Serie vs. Option. **Kein Preisvergleich**, Preise sind out of scope. | Herstellerseiten, Tests |
| **(b) Kunden- und Pressefeedback** | Was an den Wettbewerbern gelobt und kritisiert wird. Das ist der Kern deiner Frage. | Fachpresse (Autocar, What Car, ADAC, Car and Driver, Edmunds …), Besitzerbewertungen, JD Power und Consumer Reports, wo verfügbar |
| **(c) BMW-Verbatims, die Wettbewerber nennen** | Mit wem die Kunden selbst vergleichen, plus direkte Vergleiche wie *„Mercedes hat die bessere Klimaanlage“* | Unsere Feedback-Dateien |

Zu Ebene (c) habe ich schon vorab gezählt: Die Zahlen sind **rohe Treffer einer Mustersuche** mit Fehltreffern, etwa „Golf“ im Sinne von Golftasche, „Competition“ als M-Ausstattung oder „other cars“.

| Datei | Rohtreffer | Was auffällt |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| F70 | ~92 | VW, Mercedes, Audi, Mini; fast alles aus GB |
| G60 | ~178 | Tesla 62 (alle USA, vor allem Laden und Reichweite), Mercedes 32, Audi 25 |
| G70 | ~197 | Mercedes 98 (USA), Tesla 34, Porsche und Lexus je 13 |

Ein LLM klassifiziert diese Treffer sauber. Für die USA ist die Ebene stark, für die EU dünn, und **für China gibt es sie gar nicht**.

## 3. Kern des Designs: Vergleichbarkeit

Damit wir später vergleichen können, bekommt jeder Wettbewerber-Befund dieselbe Struktur wie das BMW-Feedback:

- **Feedback-Typ:** Likes, Wants, Difficult to Use, Defect, plus „Wettbewerber-Vorteil“, „BMW-Vorteil“ oder „Gleichstand“.
- **Thema:** ca. 15 grobe Themen, zum Beispiel Infotainment und Bedienung, Fahrassistenz, Laden und Reichweite, Fahrkomfort, Sitze, Platz, Innenraumqualität, Klima und Akustik. Die 226 BMW-Topics sind für Pressetexte zu fein. Wir mappen sie auf diese groben Themen, die Studien-Attribute ebenso.
- **Pro Befund:** Fahrzeug, Markt, Wettbewerbsmodell, Aussage (paraphrasiert), Quellen-URL, Quellentyp, Datum, Evidenz-Stufe.
- **Evidenz-Stufen:** A = viele Kundenaussagen, B = Fachpresse-Test, C = Herstellerangabe, D = Ankündigung oder Prognose.

Diese Felder speisen später direkt die Pflichtfelder „Linked findings and sources“ und „Evidence level“.

## 4. Ablauf und Zeitbudget

1. **Taxonomie und Schema** festlegen: Themenliste, Mappings, JSON-Schema (ca. 30 Min.).
2. **Verbatims klassifizieren:** Ein Agent geht die rund 470 Rohtreffer durch, verwirft Fehltreffer und ordnet Wettbewerber, Typ und Thema zu.
3. **Leichter Recherche-Durchgang für alle 7 Kombis:** ein Recherche-Agent pro Kombi, parallel, alle mit demselben Ausgabeschema (ca. 1–1,5 Std.).
4. **Zusammenführen:** eine Vergleichsmatrix aus Thema × Wettbewerber × Markt, die zeigt, wo BMW vorne liegt und wo hinten.
5. **Tiefer Durchgang** nur für die Demo-Kombi des Teams.

Die Ergebnisse kommen ins Repo, nicht nach `data/`, das ist gitignored:

- `docs/competitors/`: Markdown-Zusammenfassung pro Kombi
- `competitors/findings.json`: der Datensatz für die App
- `competitors/themes.json`: die Mappings

## 5. Risiken

- **China:** Die besten Quellen wären chinesische Besitzerplattformen wie Autohome oder Dongchedi. Die sind schwer abrufbar und auf Chinesisch. Ausweichen würden wir auf englische China-Fachmedien (CarNewsChina, CnEVPost) und JD Power China. Diese Daten sind dünner, das schreiben wir offen dazu.
- **Skalen:** Externe Bewertungen nutzen andere Skalen als die BMW-Studie. Wir verwenden sie nur als relatives Signal und vermischen keine Zahlen.
- **Urheberrecht:** Wir speichern nur Paraphrasen, URLs und kurze Zitate. Review-Seiten werden nicht massenhaft gescrapt.

---

## Was du entscheiden musst

1. **Tiefe:** Leichter Durchgang für alle 7 Kombis, nur ein tiefer Durchgang für die Demo-Kombi, oder beides? Ich empfehle beides.
2. **Breite:** Nur deutsche Premium-Wettbewerber, oder auch Tesla, Lexus, Genesis, Lucid und chinesische EV-Marken? Für China sind die chinesischen Marken Pflicht.
3. **Format:** Datensatz für die App plus kurze Markdown-Zusammenfassung, oder nur Markdown?
4. **Demo-Kombi:** Zu welcher Kombi tendiert das Team? Davon hängt ab, wo der tiefe Durchgang hingeht.

# Competitor research — BMW 5 Series (G60, China: G68)

Competitor vehicles for the 5 Series and what their customers and the press say about them, structured so it can be compared with BMW's own G60 feedback.

| Market | BMW baseline | Competitor feedback sources |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EU | G60 feedback (thin, mostly GB/SE/DK) + DE option list | owner reviews, owner forums, press tests |
| US | G60 feedback (rich, Sources A–D) | owner reviews, owner forums, press tests |
| CN | **G68** (long wheelbase) — no BMW feedback, so G68 owner reviews are collected from the web as baseline | Autohome / Dongchedi / Sohu / Yiche owner reviews, press |

## How comparability works

1. **Same theme axis.** [`themes.json`](themes.json) defines 18 coarse themes. Every BMW VFC level2 topic is mapped to one theme ([`tools/build_themes.py`](tools/build_themes.py)), and every competitor finding is tagged with a theme from the same list.
2. **Same feedback types** as BMW: `Likes`, `Wants`, `Difficult to Use`, `Defect`.
3. **One topic per record.** Like the BMW files (one row per classification), a review that covers three topics becomes three records sharing one `review_ref`. Count unique `review_ref`s, not records.
4. **Compare shares, not counts.** Competitor owner-review volume is far smaller than BMW's. Compare the sentiment mix per theme. The closest BMW baseline for competitor owner reviews is **BMW Source A** (owner reviews); Sources B–D (dealer/survey channels) have no competitor equivalent.
5. **Same generation.** All model years of the current generation count; the generation code is on every record.

## Files

| File | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `themes.json` | Theme taxonomy, VFC → theme mapping, feedback types, evidence tiers |
| `raw/<agent>.jsonl` | Records from one research agent (one JSON object per line) |
| `raw/<agent>.log.md` | What that agent searched, fetched, found and could not access |
| `tools/` | Scripts (theme build, merge, validation) |

## Record schema (`raw/*.jsonl`)

### `kind: "feedback"`: one statement about one theme

| Field | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `record_id` | str | `<agent>-F0001` |
| `review_ref` | str | `<agent>-R001`: groups records from the same review/post |
| `kind` | `"feedback"` | |
| `market` | `EU` \| `US` \| `CN` | |
| `country` | ISO-2 | country of the source/reviewer if known (`GB`, `DE`, `US`, `CN`, …) |
| `brand`, `model`, `generation` | str | e.g. `Mercedes-Benz`, `E-Class`, `W214` |
| `model_year` | str \| null | |
| `powertrain` | `ICE` \| `PHEV` \| `BEV` \| `unknown` | |
| `source_type` | `owner_review` \| `owner_forum` \| `owner_survey` \| `press_review` | |
| `source_name` | str | e.g. `cars.com`, `Autohome`, `Car and Driver` |
| `url` | str | **a page the agent fetched itself** |
| `published` | `YYYY-MM` \| `YYYY` \| null | |
| `feedback_type` | `Likes` \| `Wants` \| `Difficult to Use` \| `Defect` | `Wants` = request/missing feature; `Difficult to Use` = usability pain or weak performance; `Defect` = something broken |
| `theme` | theme id | from `themes.json` |
| `vfc_level2` | str \| null | best-matching BMW VFC level2 topic (keys of `vfc_level2_to_theme`), if one fits well |
| `comparison` | `competitor_advantage` \| `bmw_advantage` \| `parity` \| null | only when the source explicitly compares with BMW / the 5 Series |
| `statement` | str | English paraphrase, 1–2 sentences, one topic, e.g. "Owner states the air suspension makes the ride very smooth on highways." |
| `quote` | str \| null | optional original-language excerpt, **under 15 words** |
| `language` | `en` \| `de` \| `zh` \| … | language of the source |
| `rating` | str \| null | e.g. `4/5` if the review carries one |
| `evidence_tier` | `A` \| `B` | A = customer voice, B = press |

### `kind: "equipment"`: one customer-facing feature of one vehicle in one market

`record_id` (`<agent>-E0001`), `kind`, `market`, `brand`, `model`, `generation`, `trim_scope` (e.g. `entry trim`, `all trims`, `i5 eDrive40`), `feature`, `theme`, `availability` (`standard` \| `optional` \| `not_available` \| `unknown`), `value` (e.g. `"270 kW DC peak"`), `source_type` (`manufacturer` \| `press_review`), `url`, `as_of` (`YYYY-MM`), `evidence_tier` (`C` \| `B`), `notes`.

### `kind: "competitor"`: why a vehicle is in the competitor set

`record_id` (`<agent>-C001`), `kind`, `market`, `brand`, `model`, `generation`, `powertrains`, `launched`, `rationale`, `next_generation` (announced successor/facelift, or null), `next_generation_evidence_tier` (`D`), `url`.

## Rules for collection

- Every record cites a URL that was actually fetched. Search snippets are not records. Zero results is a valid outcome; it gets logged.
- No CAPTCHA, login or bot-block workarounds. Known blocked: Edmunds (403), Reddit, What Car (paywall).
- Store paraphrases, not copied review text; quotes stay under 15 words.
- BMW verbatim text from `data/` never goes into committed files, only IDs and labels.

"""Aggregate BMW G60 feedback onto the shared theme axis (counts only, no verbatim text).

Writes competitors/bmw_g60_theme_profile.csv with one row per
market x source x engine type x theme x feedback type, counting unique feedback IDs.

Usage: .venv/bin/python competitors/tools/bmw_baseline.py data/G60_feedback_hackathon.xlsx
"""

import json
import sys
import warnings
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
EUROPE = {"GB", "SE", "DK", "FI", "NO", "FR", "ES", "LV", "DE", "IT", "NL", "BE", "AT", "CH", "PL"}


def market(country: str) -> str:
    if country == "US":
        return "US"
    if country in EUROPE:
        return "EU"
    return "other"


def main(feedback_path: str) -> None:
    themes = json.loads((ROOT / "themes.json").read_text())
    l2_map = themes["vfc_level2_to_theme"]
    l3_map = themes["vfc_level3_to_theme"]

    df = pd.read_excel(feedback_path, dtype=str)
    df["Vfc level2 Name"] = df["Vfc level2 Name"].str.replace("\xa0", " ")

    def theme(row) -> str:
        if row["Vfc level3 Name"] in l3_map:
            return l3_map[row["Vfc level3 Name"]]
        return l2_map.get(row["Vfc level2 Name"], "unclassified")

    df["theme"] = df.apply(theme, axis=1)
    df["market"] = df["Country"].map(market)
    df["engine"] = df["Engine Type"].replace({"BEVE": "BEV"})
    df["feedback_type"] = df["Feedback Type"].fillna("none")

    profile = (
        df.drop_duplicates(["ID", "theme", "feedback_type"])
        .groupby(["market", "Source", "engine", "theme", "feedback_type"])["ID"]
        .nunique()
        .rename("feedbacks")
        .reset_index()
        .rename(columns={"Source": "source"})
    )
    out = ROOT / "bmw_g60_theme_profile.csv"
    profile.to_csv(out, index=False)

    pivot = profile.pivot_table(index="theme", columns="market", values="feedbacks", aggfunc="sum", fill_value=0)
    print(pivot.sort_values("US", ascending=False).to_string())
    print(f"wrote {out} ({len(profile)} rows)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(sys.argv[1])
